**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Lead
**Re:** Local AI hardware — expansion vs. utilisation

We've been running into capacity constraints on our local GPU fleet for about six weeks now. Jobs queue, experiments stall, and the natural instinct is to reach for a purchase order. Before we do that, I want to lay out the case for the alternative: squeezing more out of the hardware we already own. My recommendation, stated up front, is that we spend the next four to six weeks on utilisation work before committing to any new hardware, and that we treat that work as a diagnostic that will tell us whether buying is even the right move.

The cost picture is the obvious starting point. New accelerators are expensive not just at purchase but in the surrounding costs: power, cooling, rack space, and the engineering time to integrate and maintain them. Our current fleet is depreciating whether we use it or not, so every job we can fit onto existing silicon is effectively free at the margin. If our utilisation is sitting where I suspect it is — well below what the hardware could theoretically sustain — then a meaningful fraction of our capacity problem is self-inflicted. Buying more machines to solve a scheduling problem would be paying twice for the same capability.

Latency is the counterargument, and it's a fair one. Queues aren't just an efficiency issue; they're a friction tax on every engineer's day. A job that waits four hours for a slot changes how people work — they batch conservatively, avoid exploratory runs, and sometimes give up on ideas entirely. That hidden cost is real and doesn't show up on any invoice. If our utilisation problem is actually a contention problem, with a handful of long-running jobs monopolising devices while everyone else waits, then better scheduling could deliver most of the latency win without new capital. But if the fleet is genuinely saturated — every GPU busy with useful work around the clock — then no amount of scheduling cleverness will conjure capacity, and the case for buying gets much stronger. That's precisely the question we can't currently answer, because we lack the instrumentation to distinguish saturation from poor allocation.

Reliability cuts both ways. More hardware means more failure surface: more cards to fail, more thermal and power events, more maintenance windows. Our existing fleet has known quirks, and we've built operational muscle around them. Adding capacity multiplies the number of things that can go wrong before we've demonstrated we can operate what we have reliably. Conversely, pushing utilisation harder puts more stress on aging hardware and leaves less headroom for failures — if we run everything at 95% and a card dies, we have no buffer. Any utilisation push needs to preserve some deliberate slack, which is another reason to measure before we maximise.

The opportunity cost argument is, I think, the decisive one. The engineering time to build proper telemetry, a job queue with priorities, and maybe some checkpointing so long jobs can be preempted is real — it's perhaps two to three weeks of one or two engineers. But that work is valuable regardless of what we decide afterward. If we end up buying hardware, we'll want the instrumentation to justify it and the scheduler to absorb the new capacity efficiently. If we don't buy, we've permanently improved the fleet we have. Compare that to the alternative: money spent on hardware is spent, and if the demand we're seeing turns out to be a temporary spike — a push toward a deadline, a burst of experimentation — we'll own capacity we don't need. Hardware purchases are largely irreversible; scheduling improvements are not.

On reversibility more broadly: the utilisation path keeps our options open. We can revisit the purchase decision in six weeks with real data in hand, and if demand has grown since, we'll buy with confidence rather than anxiety. The purchase path forecloses options — budget committed, space consumed, and a psychological commitment to "more hardware" as the answer to future constraints.

I want to be honest about the uncertainty here. I could be wrong about our utilisation numbers; if we're already at 80%+ on useful work, this memo is arguing for a delay we can't afford, and we should escalate the purchase immediately. That's why the first week of this plan is purely measurement: instrument the fleet, get honest numbers on utilisation, queue depth, and job profiles, and reconvene. If the data says we're saturated, I'll champion the purchase with the evidence to back it. If the data says we're leaving capacity idle, we'll have fixed part of the problem for the cost of some engineering time.

Let's discuss at Thursday's sync. I'd like agreement on the measurement phase this week, with a hard checkpoint two weeks out to decide whether this becomes a build effort or a buy effort.

**MEMO**

**To:** Platform Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Working Group
**Re:** GPU capacity — buy more, or use what we have better?
**Status:** For discussion at Thursday's planning session

---

We've reached the point in our growth curve where the question can no longer be deferred: do we purchase additional local AI hardware, or do we invest in raising the utilisation of the hardware we already own? I want to lay out my thinking ahead of Thursday so we can spend the meeting deciding rather than framing.

Let me start with the honest baseline. Our current fleet sits at roughly 40–45% utilisation by most measures, though that number deserves scrutiny. A significant share of the idle time is structural rather than incidental — long-running inference jobs that hold memory between bursts, batch windows we've never tuned, and a scheduling setup that treats our four nodes as silos rather than a pool. In other words, the headline number overstates how much genuinely free capacity we have, but it also understates how much capacity we could free with focused work. The distinction matters, because the two options on the table are not really "buy" versus "do nothing."

On the cost side, the case for buying is straightforward on paper. Hardware prices have stabilised, our vendor relationship gives us a reasonable discount, and capital expenditure is easier to justify internally than headcount. But the true cost of a new node is never just the invoice. There is power and cooling, which our facilities team tells us is closer to capacity than we'd like; there is the operational burden of provisioning, monitoring, and eventually decommissioning; and there is the depreciation risk inherent in a market where accelerator generations turn over every eighteen to twenty-four months. A node bought today at full price may be worth a fraction of that as surplus in two years. That depreciation risk is real, and it argues for buying only when we're confident the demand is durable.

The case for improving utilisation is, I think, stronger than it first appears, but it is not free either. The engineering work involved — a proper job scheduler, shared-memory pooling, better queueing for batch work, and the unglamorous monitoring to actually see where capacity goes — is perhaps six to eight weeks of focused effort from two engineers. That is a genuine opportunity cost: those are the same people we'd otherwise assign to the model-quality workstream, and delaying that has its own price in team morale and roadmap slippage. We should not pretend that "use what we have" costs nothing. It costs attention, and attention is our scarcest resource.

On latency, the picture is mixed. More hardware would reduce queue times for interactive workloads immediately, which matters for the demo commitments we've made to the product team. Better scheduling could achieve much of the same effect, but with a lag, and with some risk that the scheduler itself introduces jitter in its early weeks. If we have hard latency commitments in the next quarter, that asymmetry — immediate relief from buying versus delayed and slightly uncertain relief from tuning — is the strongest argument on the purchase side, and I don't want to minimise it.

Reliability cuts the other way. A larger fleet of identical, lightly-used nodes is more resilient in one sense — more redundancy — but our failure history suggests our outages have been configuration and driver problems, not capacity exhaustion. Adding nodes multiplies the surface on which those failures occur. Better utilisation, done well, usually means better instrumentation, and better instrumentation means we detect degradation earlier. There is a reliability dividend hidden in the utilisation path that the purchase path doesn't offer.

Finally, reversibility. This is, for me, the decisive consideration. Buying a node is a largely irreversible commitment — capital spent, depreciation clock running, facilities load locked in. Investing in scheduling and instrumentation is reversible in the best sense: the skills, tooling, and monitoring we build retain their value regardless of what we later decide, and if the work reveals that our demand genuinely exceeds capacity, we will then buy with much better evidence about what to buy and how much. The utilisation path is not merely cheaper; it is an information-generating investment that de-risks the purchase we may eventually need to make.

So my recommendation is this: defer the purchase for one quarter, commit two engineers to the scheduling and instrumentation work, and set a concrete trigger — sustained utilisation above 75% with queue-time SLA breaches — at which we buy without further debate. I hold this recommendation with real uncertainty. If the product team's latency commitments are harder than I believe, or if the scheduler work stalls, we should revisit within six weeks rather than waiting out the quarter. The worst outcome is not choosing wrong; it is choosing slowly, paying for idle silicon while we deliberate.

I'd welcome pushback before Thursday, particularly from anyone with visibility into Q3 demand that I lack.
